title: Stills or motion
statement: Stills or motion: in some studies still pictures with printed text teach as well as narrated animation, but across many, animation wins on average.
detail:
Finding 1 of the film study (`othello-unit-video/research/FINDINGS.md`): static diagrams with printed text did as well
as narrated animation or better on 4 of 8 comparisons (Mayer et al. 2005, https://doi.org/10.1037/1076-898X.11.4.256),
but across 26 studies animation beat still pictures on average (Höffler & Leutner 2007,
https://doi.org/10.1016/j.learninstruc.2007.09.013), and on my own per-shot test an animated version matched its
narration for more of its screen time, 51% to 41%. To settle it: the same script and voice over stills and over
realistic video, compared on first-try answers to the same checks.

evidence.quote: Moving, speaking synthetic humans still read as fake.

Use a few richly composed panels, giving students time to inspect expressions, relationships and setting. Advance between panels rather than continuously animating them.
The target is a cinematic, narrated comic sequence with still artwork, not panels the student has to read through manually.
an illustrated book brought to life through voiceover

**Evidence.** Animation beats static imagery by *d*=0.37 overall, with representational animation at *d*=0.40, realistic/video at *d*=0.76, and procedural-motor content at *d*=1.06; decorational animation is *d*=-0.05 [8].
Route structure, parts, and comparison to progressive static diagrams; route process, transformation, and causal chains to representational animation; route real appearance to realistic footage.
Animation superiority is conditional: it helps when motion carries content and can hurt when transience or decoration dominates
